segments: One image standard, two entirely different philosophies. Understand dockerd and the daemonless model, and you understand the present and future of container engines.
Docker popularized image and container workflows and helped establish the OCI standards. Podman follows the same standards but reimplements them with a completely different architecture.
Architecture comparison: a concierge vs doing it yourself
dockerd runs continuously; resource usage depends on workload
No persistent central daemon; containers still have processes such as conmon
Traditionally a rootful daemon; rootless is also supported
Supports rootful and rootless, depending on the running user and configuration
An unavailable daemon affects management; live-restore helps in some runtime scenarios
No persistent central daemon is required, but containers still share the host kernel and resources
dockerd starts at boot; containers use restart policies
dockerd's REST API (the socket is an attack surface)
Optional Podman API and Docker-compatible API services/sockets; all require controlled permissions
daemon/containerd/shim cooperate to control the lifecycle
Docker is like staying in a hotel: the front desk (dockerd) is staffed 24 hours a day, and everything (check-in, check-out, room service) goes through it. The front desk has a master key (root).

Podman is like living in your own house: you open the door, turn off the lights, and cook for yourself. Local operations do not need a continuously staffed front desk; rootful operation or an API socket can still grant high privileges.
Common syntax is shared; verify advanced BuildKit features and version support. podman build reads Dockerfiles directly
Not supported by Podman; use Kubernetes workflows or other orchestration. generate kube only produces compatible configuration fragments, not a direct deployment migration
Common areas of interoperability (still verify by version):
Basic CLI commands (run, ps, stop, pull, push, build)
Port mapping (subject to rootless port restrictions)
Differences in implementation support for Compose deploy; deploy.resources is not exclusive to Swarm and cannot be declared unsupported across the board
Multi-driver builds with docker buildx (Podman uses podman build --platform)
docker context (Docker's feature for switching between multiple environments)

A user who controls the rootful Docker API can generally obtain capabilities close to host root; a rootless API is limited to the corresponding user's privileges. A rootful administrator can access sensitive host content through operations such as privileged mounts. Rootless operation does not thereby grant arbitrary file-read access

In rootless Podman, container UID 0 usually maps to the launching user, while other UIDs can map to subordinate IDs. This reduces exposure of host root, but user files, mounts, sockets, and kernel vulnerabilities still present risks
Open source with similar common commands; verify interoperability for the actual workload
No persistent central daemon, with rootless available; measure resource use and security in practice
Stay consistent and reduce collaboration friction
Enterprise support and mature CI/CD integration
systemd management, automatic restarts, and unified logging
Define privilege, isolation, and compatibility requirements clearly

Docker began popularizing container image workflows in 2013. The OCI was established in 2015 and accepted contributions including runc. Podman subsequently developed into an OCI engine emphasizing local operation without a persistent central daemon and support for rootless operation. Quadlet, networking, API, and Desktop features continue to evolve; a particular major version number should not be treated as the point when all features first appeared.

Docker Desktop licensing, Hub quotas, and distribution defaults can change; they do not prove container-format compatibility. Check a distribution's default engine and the requirements for coexistence on one machine against actual packages, sockets, and version configuration. Choosing an engine requires checking the actual version, container configuration, and team toolchain.
Coexistence: Docker and Podman on the same machine

Docker and Podman share common image standards, registries, and Dockerfile workflows, but their privilege models, APIs, build features, and orchestration are not guaranteed to be fully interchangeable. Choose based on security boundaries, team tooling, platform, and maintenance approach, and test compatibility with the actual application when necessary. Daemonless operation is not an absolute security guarantee, and rootless operation is not unique to Podman.
